name: Navinder Sarao

summary.text: Navinder Singh Sarao is a British futures trader who was charged by the U.S. Department of Justice in February 2015 and arrested in London in April 2015 over spoofing in E-mini S&P 500 futures between 2010 and 2015, conduct that prosecutors and the CFTC said contributed to the market conditions on the day of the 6 May 2010 'flash crash'. He pleaded guilty in Chicago in November 2016 to one count of wire fraud and one count of spoofing and was sentenced in January 2020 to time served and a year of home confinement. The CFTC and SEC staff report of 30 September 2010 attributed the crash's trigger to a 75,000-contract sell program by a large fundamental trader, not to Sarao.

facts.claim: A federal criminal complaint filed in the Northern District of Illinois on February 11, 2015 charged Sarao with one count of wire fraud, ten counts of commodities fraud, ten counts of commodities manipulation and one count of spoofing; he was arrested at his home in London on April 21, 2015 at the Justice Department's request.
facts.quote: The charges included one count of wire fraud, 10 counts of commodities fraud, 10 counts of commodities manipulation, and one count of "spoofing," a practice of bidding or offering with the intent to cancel the bid or offer before execution.

sources.title: Futures Trader Charged with Illegally Manipulating Stock Market, Contributing to the May 2010 Market 'Flash Crash'
Criminal Complaint, United States v. Navinder Singh Sarao

facts.claim: The CFTC's civil complaint, filed under seal on April 17, 2015, alleged that Sarao's manipulative activity contributed to an extreme E-mini S&P order book imbalance that helped create the market conditions that led to the flash crash, and described a 'layering' algorithm and manual 'flash' orders placed and quickly cancelled.
facts.quote: contributed to an extreme E-mini S&P order book imbalance, which helped create the market conditions that led to the Flash Crash

facts.claim: After extradition to the United States on November 7, 2016, Sarao pleaded guilty on November 9, 2016 before U.S. District Judge Virginia Kendall to one count of wire fraud and one count of spoofing, admitting illicit gains of at least $12.8 million.
facts.quote: pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Virginia Kendall in the Northern District of Illinois to one count of wire fraud and one count of spoofing

facts.claim: In November 2016 the federal court in Chicago entered a consent order in the CFTC's civil action requiring Sarao to pay more than $38 million in monetary sanctions for price manipulation and spoofing.
facts.quote: Federal Court in Chicago Orders U.K. Resident Navinder Singh Sarao to Pay More than $38 Million in Monetary Sanctions for Price Manipulation and Spoofing

facts.claim: On January 28, 2020 Judge Kendall sentenced Sarao to time served, with one year of home confinement as a condition of release; prosecutors had cited his extensive cooperation in other market-manipulation cases.
facts.quote: On January 28, 2020, Chicago-based U.S. federal district court judge Virginia Kendall sentenced Mr. Sarao to "time served," with a condition of release being one year of home confinement.

facts.claim: The CFTC and SEC staff report of September 30, 2010 found that at 2:32 p.m. on May 6, 2010 a large fundamental trader, a mutual fund complex, began a program to sell 75,000 E-Mini contracts valued at about $4.1 billion as a hedge to an existing equity position; the report did not name the firm or mention Sarao.
facts.quote: a large fundamental trader (a mutual fund complex) initiated a sell program to sell a total of 75,000 E-Mini contracts (valued at approximately $4.1 billion) as a hedge to an existing equity position

facts.claim: A CFTC Office of the Chief Economist working paper on the flash crash concluded that high-frequency traders did not cause the crash but contributed to it by demanding immediacy ahead of other market participants.
facts.quote: High Frequency Traders (HFTs) did not cause the Flash Crash, but contributed to it by demanding immediacy ahead of other market participants.

sources.title: The Flash Crash: The Impact of High Frequency Trading on an Electronic Market

openQuestions: The site names Waddell & Reed as the firm behind the $4.1 billion sell order. The CFTC/SEC report refers only to 'a large fundamental trader (a mutual fund complex)'; the identification of Waddell & Reed came from press reporting, which was not among the sources returned.

No source returned states any relationship between Sarao and Eric Hunsader or Nanex, so no connection to eric-hunsader is recorded. Hunsader's firm published quote-stuffing analyses of May 6, 2010 (ProPublica, 2010; CounterPunch, 2010) and criticized the regulators' report; those belong in an eric-hunsader file if the owner wants one.

The site's figures for cancelled trades (about 20,000 trades in 300-plus securities more than 60 percent from pre-crash prices) and the 'penny or $100,000' executions were not checked against the report text retrieved.
Sarao's sentencing exposure is given as more than 100 years in one source and up to eight years in another; the difference reflects the original complaint counts versus the two plea counts.
The entity id eric-hunsader is typed 'unknown' in entities.json; he is a person (founder of Nanex).
